name: Fatima Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Fatima. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a startup of twelve people that makes route-planning software for small courier firms, the kind with five or ten vans. I build the phone app the drivers use, so the screens that show the next stop and let them take a photo when they drop a parcel. Most mornings I'm working through bug reports from drivers, which are written in capitals and very angry, and in the afternoon I build new bits with an AI assistant open next to my code the whole time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You use the AI assistant all day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All day, every day. I ask it to draft a screen, then I fix what it gets wrong, which is a lot. To be honest, I'm not the strongest coder on the team, I came through a two-year college course, and the assistant is how I keep up. The scary part is that sometimes I ship code I couldn't fully explain if someone asked.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that real drivers use what I make; my cousin Emre drives for one of our customers and he sends me screenshots when something's broken. What wears me out is the startup feeling. We have funding until about next autumn, and every month the founders do a meeting about runway, which is how long the money lasts. I share a flat with my friend Noor and I've got maybe two weeks of rent saved, so those meetings land hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: the tools are great helpers, not magic. I'd probably post a thread saying the hype was about selling to investors, and the real win was boring stuff like writing tests faster. People who said AI would replace all of us owe everyone an apology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing really gets better for me. The startup still might run out of money next autumn, and that's a much bigger threat to me than any robot. There are only a couple of software companies in my town, so if we fold I'd be applying for remote jobs against thousands of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant but I'd make myself understand every line before I ship it, because if the magic isn't coming I need to actually be good. I'd do one online course on mobile app basics in the evenings, the free one, not the paid one. And I'd start a little side gig fixing websites for local shops, maybe two a month, to build some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of flat. I was half excited about what AI could do, so it's a bit disappointing, and the money worry is still sitting there. Funny that the thing I'd lose sleep over is a spreadsheet the founders show us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you if the startup does run out of money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have about two weeks before I'm behind on rent. Noor would cover me for a month, she's said so, but I'd hate that. My parents are not in a position to help; my dad's a bus driver and they're still paying off their own flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should carry that risk, you or the founders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not me, that's for sure. The founders own the company, they get the upside, but if it fails we all lose our jobs the same day with almost nothing. I think startups should have to keep a few months of wages aside for staff, and I'd vote for anyone who made that a rule.

say: AI tools are **great helpers**, not magic, and the hype was about selling to **investors**.
The real gains were **boring tasks**, like writing tests faster.
think: The startup running out of money **next autumn** is a bigger threat than AI.
With only a couple of local software firms, I'd face **thousands** of remote applicants.
do: Understand **every line** of code before shipping it, instead of trusting the assistant.
Take a **free online course** on mobile app basics in the evenings.
Fix **websites for local shops**, about two a month, to build savings.
feel: **Flat** and a bit **disappointed**, with the money worry still sitting there.
S0.quote: The startup still might run out of money next autumn, and that's a much bigger threat to me than any robot.
fieldNote: Fatima's main risk is the **startup's runway**, not AI; that keeps her anxious even here.

She wants a rule forcing startups to hold **wages in reserve** for staff.

steps.text: Read and understand every line the assistant writes before shipping it
Take the free online course on mobile app basics
Fix websites for local shops, about two jobs a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for developers to stop thinking we're special and start acting like workers. Coding is on the list, same as customer service. Online I'd push for a tech workers' union and for the companies saving money to pay into retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in a weird spot. I'm already good with the AI tools, better than some seniors who refuse to touch them, so in a small team I might be the one they keep. But I'm also weak on the fundamentals, and if the tools write good code on their own, a junior like me is just an extra cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the tools, but at a higher level: learning how to set up the AI agents that write and test code, not just chatting with one. I'd pitch the founders on letting me run that for the team within the first three months. At the same time I'd apply to a couple of remote jobs a month so I'm not trapped if we fold, and I'd go to the tech workers' meetup in the city once a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and a bit buzzing at the same time. I like change, I really do, but I also know I'm one bad funding round from no job at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might be the one they keep. What makes you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because last month our lead spent a whole day doing by hand what I did with the assistant in an hour. Viktor noticed, and he asked me to show him. That's the first time a senior has asked me to teach them anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if your hours or pay drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out with Noor, which we do every Friday, and my gym. After that, I'd probably move back in with my parents for a bit, even though their flat is tiny and I'd be sleeping in my old room with my little sister's things everywhere.

say: Developers should stop thinking we're **special** and start acting like **workers**.
Companies saving money with AI should pay into **retraining** and accept a tech union.
think: Being good with **AI tools** might make me the one a small team keeps.
My **weak fundamentals** mean that once tools code well alone, I'm just an extra cost.
do: Learn to set up **AI agents** that write and test code, and pitch running it within three months.
Apply to **two remote jobs** a month as a backup.
Attend the monthly **tech workers' meetup** in the city.
feel: **Nervous and buzzing** at once: she likes change but fears one bad funding round.
S1.quote: Last month our lead spent a whole day doing by hand what I did with the assistant in an hour.
fieldNote: Fatima's edge is **tool skill** that seniors lack; it gave her status for the first time.
She sees the trap clearly: the same tools could make **juniors redundant**.
Moving back to her **parents' tiny flat** is her real fallback.

steps.text: Learn to run AI agents that write and test the drivers' app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political emergency, not a tech story. We'd need income support for everyone, fast, and the AI companies taxed hard to pay for it. I'd be organising online, and probably on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I think my job is gone. Everything I do is at a screen, there's no hands-on part to hide in, so 2028 is my date, not 2031. My advantage with the tools lasts maybe a year, until the tools don't need someone like me to drive them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next two years I'd squeeze every bit of money and skill out of this job I can, and save hard, even if that means moving back with my parents to bank the rent. I'd learn how these systems get checked and approved, because someone has to sign off on what the AI does, at least for a while. And I'd put real hours into the campaign for income support, because no personal plan beats two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry underneath it. I'd feel like I did everything right, learned the new thing early, and it still wouldn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots coming three years later? Does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only as an escape route. My cousin Emre drives a van, so his job lasts until about 2031, longer than mine. I've actually thought I could go drive with him, which is mad after two years of college, but three years of wages is three years of wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm coming home for a while and it's not because I failed. My mum would make it into a big family thing. My dad would quietly ask if the bus company is hiring, which honestly, maybe.

say: This is a **political emergency**, needing fast **income support** for everyone.
AI companies should be **taxed hard** to pay for it, and I'd organise online and on the street.
think: All my work is at a screen, so **2028**, not 2031, is my date.
My edge with the tools lasts **maybe a year**, until they don't need a driver.
do: Move back with her parents to **save the rent** for two years.
Learn how AI work gets **checked and approved**, aiming for sign-off roles.
Put real hours into the **income support** campaign.
feel: **Frightened and angry**: she learned the new tools early, and it still wouldn't matter.
S2.quote: Everything I do is at a screen, there's no hands-on part to hide in, so 2028 is my date, not 2031.
fieldNote: Fatima reads the **robot delay** as a lifeline for others, like her van-driving cousin, not for her.
Being an **early adopter** buys her a year at most, and she knows it.
Her anger is at being **punished for adapting**, a sharp reversal from earlier scenarios.

steps.text: Move back into her parents' flat to save rent
Study how AI-written code gets reviewed and approved
Organise for income support funded by taxing AI companies
Ask cousin Emre about driving vans as a fallback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one: income support and taxing the gains. But with five years I'd add that we should be building the support now, not after. I'd be a bit less shouty and a bit more organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get a few good years in software, maybe even a promotion, if I'm the one who runs the AI for the team. Then 2031 arrives and it's over for screen work. Five years is long enough to build something, but not long enough to feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first two or three years I'd become the AI person at work and try to get a mid-level title, because that raises my pay and makes my next move easier. I'd save properly, aiming for three months by 2028. And I'd take a part-time course in something people still want a human for, maybe social work, because I've always liked helping people, and robots for that kind of work only come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with some energy in it. Five years feels like a race I could actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Social work is a big switch from coding. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt is a social worker, and the parts of her job that are paperwork would go, but the visiting families part wouldn't, not soon. I'm good with people, better than I am with code, if I'm honest. And it pays about the same as I earn now, which says a lot about my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you're weak on fundamentals. Does that worry you in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less, because in five years nobody's going to care if I can write a sorting algorithm by hand. They'll care if I can make the AI do the right thing and explain it to a manager. That's the part I'm actually good at.

Five years means being **less shouty** and more organised about policy.
think: A few good years in software, maybe a **promotion**, if I run the AI for the team.

S3.quote: Five years feels like a race I could actually run.
fieldNote: With five years Fatima plans a **two-step** career: AI lead first, then social work.

steps.text: Run the team's AI coding agents and push for a mid-level title

Join the campaign to build income support before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. Shorter weeks, retraining paid for by the companies, a basic income trial or two. I'd be the annoying person at every party talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd honestly be okay in this one, I think. Ten years of being the one who's good with the tools is a whole career stage. I'd be thirty-seven, probably with real savings, and time to switch to something people-facing before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in software and aim to lead how a team works with AI by 2030. I'd keep the shop-website side gig going, because a second income matters when you've got nothing saved. I'd start the social work idea slowly, maybe a short course around 2031, once I can see which way things are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a small knot in my stomach. The knot is the startup's money, honestly, more than AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the knot is the startup's money. Even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because AGI in 2036 doesn't help if the startup folds next autumn. Ten years is a long time if you have a job. If I don't, it's one month at a time like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the founders to do with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell us the truth about the plan, every quarter, and train us on whatever they're building. If they're going to replace us with AI, they should at least make sure we're the ones who know how it works when we leave.

say: Ten years is **a gift** if we use it for shorter weeks and **retraining**.
A **basic income trial** or two should start well before 2036.
think: Ten years of being good with the tools is a **whole career stage**.
The **startup folding** next autumn worries me more than AGI in 2036.

Keep the **shop-website side gig** going for a second income.
Start a short **social work** course around 2031.
feel: **Mostly excited**, with a small knot about the startup's money.
S4.quote: AGI in 2036 doesn't help if the startup folds next autumn.
fieldNote: Fatima is **uneasy** rather than calm: the ten-year world is good, but her firm's **runway** isn't.
She asks founders for **quarterly honesty** and training, not job guarantees.
Her side gig is her answer to having **no cushion**.

steps.text: Push to lead the team's AI workflow by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have two years, no savings, and a job that's all screen. What would help is income support that's already built and waiting, and paid retraining into people jobs, so nobody has to choose between a course and the rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd still choose coding. I would, actually, because it taught me how these systems think. Being early to AI doesn't save your job, but it does mean you see the wave before it hits.

headlineQuote: Being early to AI doesn't save your job, but it does mean you see the wave before it hits.
portrait: Fatima, 27, builds the **drivers' phone app** at a twelve-person startup making route software for courier firms.
She uses an **AI assistant** all day, and admits it covers for weak fundamentals she's still learning.
Her nearest threat is the startup's **runway**; she has about two weeks of rent saved.
In the AGI pictures she sees no **hands-on shelter** for herself and turns to politics and people-facing work.
With more time she plans to lead AI work, then move toward **social work** like her aunt.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: two years, no savings and a job that is all screen work.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** built in advance, plus paid retraining into jobs that need people.
